title: Reagent-Strip Chemistry: What Each Pad Sees and Misses
summary: Understand the reaction behind the blood, protein, ketone, nitrite, bilirubin and urobilinogen pads, their false positives and negatives, and the confirmatory tests — microscopy and sulfosalicylic acid — that settle a surprising result.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 29 Hits 2, 4, 9 and 12 and Traps 1, 2, 3 and 5. Checked against Simerville 2005, Sacks 2011, Umpierrez 2024 and Aitekenov 2021. Not taught: “βHB ≈ 78% of ketoacids in DKA” (Sacks 2011 describes equimolar AcAc and βHB normally, shifting toward βHB in DKA — no figure), nitrite’s “≥ 4 hours” bladder time, urobilinogen oxidation to urobilin on standing, normal urine bilirubin 0.02 mg/dL, and pad-specific read times (Trap 4) — not in the sources read.

objectives: Name the reaction behind each common dipstick pad.
List major false-positive and false-negative causes for the blood, protein, nitrite and ketone pads.
Use microscopy and sulfosalicylic acid to confirm or refute dipstick findings.
Interpret urine bilirubin and urobilinogen patterns.

scenes.title: Three strips that tell half the truth
scenes.altText: Three urine cards. Card A: blood pad 3+, microscopy 0–2 RBC/hpf. Card B: an older man with back pain and anemia; protein pad negative, but a sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) test is cloudy. Card C: a woman with dysuria; leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative. A question token: “Which pad is lying — or just not built for this?” The cartoon scientist holds a dipstick up to the light.

cues.text: Urine A: the blood pad reads 3 plus, but the microscope shows almost no red cells.
Urine B, from an older man with back pain and anemia: the protein pad is negative, yet a sulfosalicylic acid test turns cloudy.
Urine C, from a woman with painful urination: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative. Each pad reacts to one chemistry, and each has blind spots.

props.label: Lying — or not built for this?

scenes.title: Each pad is one chemical reaction
scenes.altText: A dipstick with labelled pads (schematic). Blood: peroxidase activity of heme — catalysed by intact RBCs, free hemoglobin and myoglobin. Protein: a dye sensitive mainly to albumin; may miss γ-globulins and Bence Jones proteins. Ketones: nitroprusside (with glycine) reacts with acetoacetate (and acetone) — not β-hydroxybutyrate. Nitrite: bacteria reduce dietary nitrate to nitrite; many gram-negative and some gram-positive organisms can. Bilirubin: normal urine has none detectable; only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered. Urobilinogen: small amounts are normal. A note: examine urine within 2 hours of collection.

cues.text: Each pad on a dipstick is one chemical reaction. The blood pad detects the peroxidase activity of heme, which intact red cells, free hemoglobin and myoglobin all have.
The protein pad’s dye is mainly sensitive to albumin. It may miss gamma-globulins and Bence Jones light chains.
The ketone pad uses nitroprusside. It reacts with acetoacetate and acetone, never with beta-hydroxybutyrate.
The nitrite pad needs bacteria that reduce dietary nitrate to nitrite. Many gram-negatives, and some gram-positives, can.
Normal urine has no detectable bilirubin; only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered. A little urobilinogen is normal. Test the urine within two hours.

scenes.title: False positives and false negatives, pad by pad
scenes.altText: A table builds (from Simerville 2005). Blood — false +: myoglobinuria, hemoglobinuria, menstrual blood, dehydration, exercise; false −: vitamin C, captopril, high specific gravity, pH < 5.1, proteinuria. Protein — false +: alkaline or concentrated urine, phenazopyridine, quaternary ammonium compounds; false −: acidic or dilute urine, protein other than albumin. Nitrite — false +: contamination, strips exposed to air, phenazopyridine; false −: non-nitrate-reducing organisms, high specific gravity, vitamin C, pH < 6.0, high urobilinogen. Ketones — false +: acidic urine, high specific gravity, mesna, some drug metabolites; nitroprusside misses β-hydroxybutyrate. Bilirubin — false +: phenazopyridine; false −: chlorpromazine, selenium.

cues.text: Blood pad: free hemoglobin, myoglobin and menstrual blood read positive without hematuria. Vitamin C, captopril and a high specific gravity can make it read falsely negative.
Protein pad: alkaline or concentrated urine and phenazopyridine give false positives. Dilute or acidic urine, or a protein that is not albumin, gives false negatives.
Nitrite: organisms that cannot reduce nitrate, vitamin C or a high specific gravity give false negatives. Strips left open to air give false positives.
Ketones: the pad can read positive in acidic or concentrated urine and with mesna, and it never sees beta-hydroxybutyrate.
And phenazopyridine, the orange urinary analgesic, interferes with several pads at once.

scenes.title: Confirm with the right second test
scenes.altText: A confirmation board. Blood pad positive → microscopy: intact RBCs = hematuria (≥ 3 RBC/hpf); none = hemoglobin or myoglobin. Protein: SSA precipitates all proteins — albumin and globulins, including light chains — so SSA positive with a negative pad suggests a non-albumin protein (e.g., Bence Jones), while a pad positive in very alkaline urine with negative SSA suggests a false positive. Nitrite: specific but not sensitive — a negative does not rule out UTI. Bilirubin: any detectable is abnormal → conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (liver or biliary). Urobilinogen: raised in hemolysis and hepatocellular disease; reduced in bile-duct obstruction and with antibiotics. Back to the hook: A needs microscopy (pigment), B needs protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, C may still be a UTI.

cues.text: A positive blood pad goes to the microscope. Three or more red cells per high-power field is hematuria; no cells means free hemoglobin or myoglobin.
Sulfosalicylic acid precipitates all proteins, albumin and globulins alike. SSA positive with a negative pad points to a non-albumin protein such as Bence Jones light chains.
The reverse, a positive pad in very alkaline urine with a negative SSA, suggests a false-positive pad.
Nitrite is specific but not sensitive: a negative result does not rule out infection. Any detectable bilirubin is abnormal and means conjugated bilirubin, from liver or biliary disease.
Urobilinogen rises in hemolysis and liver-cell disease and falls with bile-duct obstruction or antibiotics. So A needs microscopy, B needs protein electrophoresis, and C may still have a UTI.

scenes.title: Four classic traps
scenes.altText: Four trap cards: “Blood pad positive = red cells present” (✓ also free hemoglobin or myoglobin — check microscopy); “Negative ketone pad rules out DKA” (✓ misses β-hydroxybutyrate); “Protein pad positive in pH 8.5 urine = proteinuria” (✓ alkaline urine gives false positives — confirm with SSA); “Old specimen, normal urobilinogen” (✓ examine within 2 hours of collection).

cues.text: Trap one: a positive blood pad means red cells are present. Free hemoglobin and myoglobin do it too. Check the microscope.
Trap two: a negative ketone pad rules out DKA. It cannot see beta-hydroxybutyrate.
Trap three: a positive protein pad in urine of pH 8.5 means proteinuria. Alkaline urine causes false positives. Confirm with SSA.
Trap four: trusting a dipstick on a specimen that sat for hours. Examine urine within two hours of collection.

props.title: ✗ “Protein + at pH 8.5 = proteinuria.”
lines: ✓ Alkaline false positive — confirm with SSA

scenes.title: Every pad has one job and one blind spot
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Every pad has one job and one blind spot: blood sees heme, not cells; protein sees albumin, not light chains; ketone sees AcAc, not βHB; nitrite sees reducers, not all bacteria.” Four tokens. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: every pad has one job and one blind spot. Blood sees heme, not cells. Protein sees albumin, not light chains. Ketone sees acetoacetate, not beta-hydroxybutyrate. Nitrite sees reducers, not all bacteria.
Where it breaks: each pad has more than one interference; the protein pad can detect other proteins at high levels; and confirmation tests have their own limits.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Blood pad = heme (RBC, Hb, myoglobin) → microscopy · protein pad = albumin → SSA for all proteins · ketone pad misses βHB”, “Nitrite: specific, not sensitive · any bilirubin = abnormal · test within 2 h”.

cues.text: Know what each dipstick pad actually reacts with, confirm surprises with microscopy or SSA, and test fresh urine.

props.label: Blood = heme → microscopy · protein = albumin → SSA · ketone misses βHB
Nitrite: specific, not sensitive · any bilirubin abnormal · test within 2 h

explanation.what: Plain language: each square on a urine dipstick is a small chemistry test that reacts with one substance, so each can be fooled. Scientific terms: heme peroxidase activity, protein-error-of-indicator dye (albumin-sensitive), nitroprusside, nitrate reductase, sulfosalicylic acid (SSA) precipitation, conjugated bilirubin, urobilinogen.
explanation.why: Heme in RBCs, free hemoglobin and myoglobin all catalyse the peroxidase reaction. The protein dye responds mainly to albumin, and its colour shifts in very alkaline urine. Nitroprusside reacts with AcAc and acetone but not βHB. Nitrite requires nitrate-reducing bacteria and dietary nitrate. Only conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin is filtered.
explanation.measure: Hematuria: ≥ 3 RBC/hpf. Protein pad: trace ≈ 5–10 mg/dL, 1+ ≈ 30 mg/dL. SSA precipitates albumin and globulins (detection limit ~0.05 mg/mL). Nitrite positive implies significant bacteria (> 10,000/mL); air-exposed strips turn falsely positive (one-third after one week). Examine urine within 2 hours.
explanation.differs: Hematuria (intact RBCs) vs hemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria (no RBCs). Albuminuria (pad and SSA positive) vs light-chain proteinuria (SSA positive, pad negative) vs alkaline false positive (pad positive, SSA negative). Hemolysis (urobilinogen ↑, bilirubin −) vs obstruction (bilirubin +, urobilinogen ↓).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: heme pad without RBCs, alkaline false-positive protein, SSA for Bence Jones protein, nitroprusside missing βHB, nitrite false negatives, and bilirubin/urobilinogen patterns.

comparisons.title: Protein pad vs SSA
comparisons.distinguisher: Discordant results point to non-albumin protein or an alkaline false positive.

comparisons.title: Hemolysis vs biliary obstruction in urine
comparisons.distinguisher: Which bile pigment appears in urine.

mnemonic.text: Every pad has one job and one blind spot.
mnemonic.explanation: Blood sees heme, not cells; protein sees albumin, not light chains; ketone sees AcAc, not βHB; nitrite sees nitrate reducers, not all bacteria.
mnemonic.limitation: Each pad has several interferences; high non-albumin protein can register; confirmation tests have their own limits.

questions.stem: A urine sample has pH 8.5, protein pad 1+, and a negative sulfosalicylic acid test. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Likely false-positive protein pad from alkaline urine
options.rationale: Correct. Alkaline urine can turn the protein pad positive; SSA, which precipitates all proteins, is negative.
Incorrect. Light chains give the opposite pattern: SSA positive, pad negative.

options.text: Early glomerular proteinuria that only the pad can detect

options.rationale: Incorrect. That diagnosis needs split collections; this pattern points to a pad artefact.

questions.stem: A woman with dysuria has positive leukocyte esterase and a negative nitrite. What should the laboratory conclude about the nitrite result?

options.text: A negative nitrite does not rule out infection; some organisms do not reduce nitrate
options.rationale: Correct. Nitrite is specific but not sensitive.
Incorrect. Non-reducing organisms, dilute urine or vitamin C can give false negatives.

options.text: The leukocyte esterase must be a false positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. The two pads detect different things.

options.text: The strip was exposed to air
options.rationale: Incorrect. Air exposure causes false-positive nitrite, not false-negative.

questions.stem: A jaundiced patient’s urine is bilirubin-positive with low urobilinogen. Which condition fits best?

options.rationale: Correct. Conjugated bilirubin spills into urine while less bilirubin reaches the gut to form urobilinogen.
Incorrect. Hemolysis raises urobilinogen; unconjugated bilirubin does not enter urine.
Incorrect. Any detectable urine bilirubin is abnormal.
Incorrect. Myoglobin affects the blood pad, not bilirubin.
